_what_this_is: The standing rule that a Tier A change is reviewed by a session OTHER than the one that wrote it, made mechanical. Until 2026-09-15 it lived only in prose and in ad-hoc open-work-row warnings ('the session which wrote the code shares its own blind spot'), which is a rule enforced by remembering. Push-gate check 13 (tools/tier_a_review_gate.py) reads this file.
_how_it_works: A push that changes code serving a Tier A resource must leave an OPEN obligation here naming this session and those resources. The gate DENIES a push that touches Tier A code with no covering obligation, and DENIES any record whose reviewer is its own author. Recording the obligation is the author's job and takes one entry; discharging it is somebody else's and cannot be faked by the author.
_what_it_does_NOT_claim: That a review happened, or that it was any good. It is a record that the obligation EXISTS and was not self-signed. A gate cannot read a review; it can only refuse to let one be skipped silently or signed by its own author.
_scope: Tier A resources, derived from docs/CRITICALITY-TIERS.md. Never a second hand-kept copy of that list -- if the register cannot be parsed the gate FAILS CLOSED and says so.

records.what: Item 97: SAIRNcode's seven Tier A records moved from a destroying `delete` to `soft_delete`, with a read filter, a handler-level refusal and the client call sites repointed. RECORDED RETROACTIVELY on the day the gate was built -- the commit landed hours before check 13 existed, so nothing refused it, and leaving the first Tier A change under the new rule unrecorded would have been the exact gap the rule is about. The reviewer should look hardest at three things: whether the read filter really excludes marked rows on all seven and only those seven; whether repointing the seven client call sites missed one; and whether SC_TIER_A_SOFT_DELETE_ONLY agreeing with docs/CRITICALITY-TIERS.md is actually enforced in both directions or only one.

records.what: A LIVE SECURITY GAP: sc_denial_events is Tier A in the register and was NOT in the hand-written six-name write gate, so it accepted a write from the LICENCE KEY ALONE. Measured against the deployed function, not inferred -- the other six answered 401 NO_SESSION and sc_denial_events answered 200. SC_TIER_A_WRITE_GATED is now DERIVED from the same pinned Tier A list the removal verbs use, so the two cannot diverge again. The reviewer should look hardest at: whether deriving the write gate from the soft-delete list is the RIGHT equivalence or a coincidence that will break when a Tier A resource legitimately needs one and not the other; whether the suite's three hand-moved counts (20 ungated, 7 gated, 8 refusal-helper callers) were each re-measured or just made to pass; and whether any OTHER app has the same shape -- a hand-written gate list beside a tier register nobody compares it to. ALSO IN THIS REVIEW PASS, added 2026-09-15 rather than opening a third record for the same resources: (a) tools/sc_tier_a_write_gate_live_probe.py carried its OWN hand-written list of six and so LIVE-VERIFIED six of seven while reporting 'all six refuse' -- true, over the wrong denominator; it is derived from the registry now; (b) tools/tier_a_review_gate.py had a real FAIL-OPEN: subprocess text=True decoded git output with the cp1252 locale default, the reader thread raised UnicodeDecodeError on this repo's box-drawing characters, and the call returned TRUNCATED stdout rather than failing -- a diff-reading gate silently getting a short diff under-detects and reports clean. Encoding is explicit now. THE REVIEWER SHOULD CHECK whether any OTHER tool on this platform reads git output with a bare text=True, because the same one-line defect is invisible until the diff happens to contain a non-ASCII byte.

The item 97 under-assignment sweep. NOTE FOR THE REVIEWER: this obligation is a FALSE POSITIVE of the gate and is recorded rather than excluded. The only Tier A name in the diff is sv_audit_log, appearing as a FIXTURE STRING in tests/run_tier_a_replaceability_probe.py -- t.SHAPE.search('sv_audit_log') -- so no code serving sv_audit_log changed. The gate's documented posture is that over-inclusion costs one register entry and under-inclusion is a Tier A change slipping through clean, so the honest response is to record it; adding a tests/ exclusion would blind the gate to real test-side changes to Tier A behaviour, which is a worse trade. What DID change and is worth a look: tools/tier_a_replaceability_check.py gained --under, whose ATTESTATION signal shipped with a literal backspace (byte 0x08) and reported zero hits platform-wide until a positive control caught it, then reported zero again until it learned to resolve constant aliases. Check whether the +/-300 window is the right narrowness and whether any OTHER signal on this platform has never been asserted to FIRE on a known case.
